questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A bill of exchange and the gap it opens
questions.learningObjective: state what a bill of exchange makes possible
questions.stem: A merchant in one port sells cloth to a buyer in another and does not want to carry coin across the sea or wait for the buyer's money to travel back. He draws a written order on a named person in the buyer's town, payable there on a stated future date, and hands it to a factor who collects the buyer's payment and takes a smaller sum for his own service. Which feature is doing the work?

options.text: Payment is collected where the debt was owed and remitted by a deduction, so the coin need not cross the sea at all
The order is enforceable at two courts at once, so a buyer who refuses it can be sued in either place
options.misconception: supplies a jurisdiction the instrument does not create

options.text: The order fixes the price of the cloth, so neither party can reopen the bargain once it is signed
options.misconception: turns a payment instrument into a price contract

options.text: The order makes the factor's commission payable by the buyer in the buyer's own coin rather than the seller's
options.misconception: invents a currency clause the instrument does not require

questions.explanation: The whole invention is the decoupling of where a debt is owed from where the money has to be, and that is what the two-place clause does. The buyer pays in the town where he owes the money, the factor takes his charge at the moment of collection, and the seller receives a credit at home for the remainder, so the coin never makes the voyage and the risk of carrying it is transferred to somebody better placed to bear it. That is why the instrument is worth arranging, and also why it is a document rather than a promise: the named person on whom it is drawn has something in the buyer's town, which is the difference between an order that can be presented and a wish that cannot. The distractors each attribute a feature the instrument does not have, whether a double jurisdiction, a price effect, or a currency clause.
questions.hint: Ask where the money is actually collected, and how the seller gets the remainder.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A bill of exchange and the gap it opens
questions.learningObjective: trace what happens when a debt is not paid at the date named
questions.stem: A bill is drawn payable in a town where the named person has failed to honour it. The holder does not sue the buyer but presses the person on whom the bill was drawn, and in some towns the law allows a rate of damages fixed in advance if the bill is not paid when due. Which feature is being exploited?

options.text: The bill is an undertaking by a different party from the debtor, so the holder's claim runs against whoever gave the undertaking
The bill is a claim on the goods, so the holder can take the cloth rather than the money
options.misconception: confuses a financial instrument with a security in the goods

options.text: The bill is negotiable, so a holder who is disappointed can simply sell it to someone else at a discount
options.misconception: treats resale as a remedy against a defaulting party

options.text: The bill is sealed, so the court must enforce it whatever the parties agree privately
options.misconception: invents a formality the instrument does not require

questions.explanation: The instrument works by standing between the person who owes and the person who has given the undertaking, and that gap is what makes it more than a record of a sale. When the debtor does not pay, the holder's problem is that the debtor may be far away, and the answer the instrument supplies is that there is a named party in the holder's own town who is on the hook instead, so the holder can press a local claim rather than a foreign one. The fixed damages matter for the same reason, since they tell a party in advance what the default will cost and therefore make the undertaking worth something before anything goes wrong. The distractors each misidentify what the claim is against, or add a remedy or a formality the instrument does not have.
questions.hint: Ask who owes the holder, as against who owes the buyer.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A bill of exchange and the gap it opens
questions.learningObjective: assess the claim that an instrument removed a risk from a trade
questions.stem: A bill of exchange is widely said to have taken the risk of carrying coin across long distances out of merchant trade. A historian notes that merchants in several ports continued to insist on payment in coin on delivery, that governments repeatedly suspended their debts and forced merchants to take payment in paper instead, and that the instrument itself was the vehicle for that. Which account best fits?

options.text: The instrument shifted a risk between parties and between places rather than abolishing it, which is why the settlement of debts turned out to be as dangerous as the transport of coin
The instrument removed the risk from merchants, since a written undertaking cannot be lost at sea as coin can
options.misconception: treats a claim about the undertaking as a claim about the good's safety

options.text: The instrument is the cause of the suspensions, since paper debts are easier for a government to refuse than coin payments
options.misconception: makes a settlement instrument the cause of sovereign default

options.text: Merchants insisted on coin because they distrusted the procedure, so the instrument's uptake was slower than is usually claimed
options.misconception: explains a practice by distrust without evidence of distrust

questions.explanation: What the instrument did was move a risk from one holder to another rather than remove it from the world, and the proof of that is where the risk ended up. A claim on a named person in a distant town is only as good as that person's ability and willingness to pay, so a merchant holding a bill in a country that suspends its debts holds a claim against a debtor that has just announced it will not pay, which is a worse position than a merchant holding coin and a market to sell in. This is the same insight that governs the later history of government paper: the settlement of obligations concentrates claims, and concentration is exactly what makes a collective refusal damaging. The distractors each treat the instrument as risk-eliminating, invert the direction of causation, and explain a documented practice by an undocumented motive.
questions.hint: Ask where the risk moved to, and who the holder ends up depending on.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A bill of exchange and the gap it opens
questions.learningObjective: explain why price risk and performance risk are different problems
questions.stem: Two merchants in different towns buy and sell the same commodity. One loses because the price moved against him between the signing of a contract and the delivery of the goods, and the other loses because the buyer never paid at all. A new instrument is offered that guarantees only the second merchant against non-payment. Which claim about the loss the instrument addresses is correct?

options.text: It removes the risk of the buyer defaulting, and leaves the risk of a price movement entirely where it was
It removes both risks, since guaranteeing payment also fixes the price at which payment is made
options.misconception: supplies a price guarantee the instrument does not offer

options.text: It removes the price risk, because a fixed payment date also fixes the price at that date
options.misconception: confuses a payment date with a price determination

options.text: It halves the total exposure, since non-payment is usually the larger of the two losses
options.misconception: asserts a proportion the two cases do not establish

questions.explanation: The two losses are different in kind, which is why one can be transferred and the other cannot be by the same piece of paper. Non-payment is a question about a person's willingness or ability to pay on a date, and a named undertaking backed by a fixed penalty in a place where it can be enforced answers it. A price movement is a question about what the commodity will be worth, and nothing in an undertaking to pay makes the payer's obligation conditional on a price, so the risk stays with the party who took it. That is also why a merchant who wants both must use two devices, and why the study of these instruments is a study in which risks can be assigned and which must be carried. The distractors each add a price effect, and one asserts a proportion of the two losses that the cases do not supply.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two losses is a question about a person and which is a question about a market.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ledger that makes a claim checkable
questions.learningObjective: state the check a double entry provides
questions.stem: A firm keeps its accounts so that every transaction is entered twice, once as what the firm has received and once as what it has given up, and the two columns are kept equal. Which feature of that arrangement is the point of it?

options.text: An entry that has been made in only one place leaves the columns unequal, so a deliberate or accidental error is detectable by testing the balance
Entering a transaction twice halves the amount of paper the firm has to keep
options.misconception: treats double entry as a reduction in volume rather than a duplication

options.text: Equal columns show that the firm is solvent, since an equal set of entries cannot be a loss
options.misconception: confuses a bookkeeping identity with a measure of health

options.text: Equal columns mean the firm's prices have not changed, since changing a price would unbalance the accounts
options.misconception: supposes a price change appears as a bookkeeping imbalance

questions.explanation: The arrangement is a self-checking system, and the check is the whole of it: because each transaction has two sides, the total of what came in and the total of what went out are two independent descriptions of the same activity, so any entry made once and not twice, or made twice with different figures, shows up as a discrepancy when the columns are added. That is what turns a set of records from a list of assertions into something that can be audited by a stranger, which is the condition for using them as evidence at all. It is important to be clear about what it does not do, since it detects a mismatch rather than establishing the truth of an entry that is wrong in both columns, and a careful keeper's disciplined use of the same account for a false purpose is beyond its reach. The distractors each misread duplication as economy, and each confuse an accounting identity with a fact about the firm.
questions.hint: Ask what a single unpaired entry would do to the two columns.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ledger that makes a claim checkable
questions.learningObjective: read an archive of a firm's books as evidence
questions.stem: An archive of a large cloth merchant's correspondence and account books survives for roughly fifty years, containing thousands of letters, invoices, receipts and ledgers, kept by a firm that also had a factor in another city. Read that archive: what makes it capable of settling a question about the trade that a single merchant's memoir could not?

options.text: The books were kept continuously and by someone who had to reconcile them with a partner elsewhere, so a claim has to survive a check it was not written for
The archive is unusually long, so a fifty-year record can settle a question that a short one cannot
options.misconception: credits volume rather than the fact of independent checking

options.text: The firm was large, so its records describe the trade as a whole rather than one merchant's dealings
options.misconception: infers representativeness from the size of a firm

options.text: The letters are informal, so they record what was actually said rather than what the firm wished to record
options.misconception: treats informality as a guarantee of accuracy

questions.explanation: The archive's value is not its length and not the size of the firm, but the fact that the records were produced for an internal purpose and then had to hold up against somebody who did not make them. A merchant who wants the books to show that a sum was owed will write the entry carefully, but a set of accounts that also has to be reconciled with a partner's copy of the same transaction, and that a factor in another city reports against, contains a built-in contradiction, and a claim that is false has to survive that contradiction as well as the counterparty's. That is what makes a large body of commercial correspondence and accounts usable for questions nobody intended to ask, such as the price of a commodity in a named month or the terms on which a factor was paid. The distractors each credit volume, size, or informality, none of which is the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask who else had to be satisfied by the entries before the book was any use to the firm.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ledger that makes a claim checkable
questions.learningObjective: trace a change from keeping accounts to publishing them
questions.stem: A treatise printed in the last quarter of the fifteenth century sets out the rules of double entry in full, with worked examples, and it appears in several hundred editions within a few decades; a firm whose surviving books already use the method was established a century before it. Which feature of the sequence best explains the spread?

options.text: The method circulated as printed matter, so a practice that had taken a firm a century to develop could be copied without being reinvented
The method was invented by the author of the treatise, and the earlier firm's books show a coincidence of timing
options.misconception: supposes the treatise invented a method already in use

options.text: The number of editions measures the number of firms that adopted the method, since every copy was bought by a user
options.misconception: equates print runs with adoption

options.text: The earlier firm's books show the method spread from one city, since a practice of that kind spreads from where it begins
options.misconception: infers a place of origin from an archive's location

questions.explanation: The sequence is explained by the change in what could be copied, and the two facts are the proof: a method in use a century earlier shows that it was not invented by the treatise, and the rapid appearance of many printed editions shows that knowledge of it travelled fast and cheaply once it was printed. A practice that previously had to be transmitted by apprenticeship, by a master clerk, or by the slow accumulation of a firm's own experience could now be acquired by reading, which converts an institutional advantage into a portable technique. That is a general pattern in the history of technique, and it is worth holding onto precisely because a printing revolution is often described as though it chiefly multiplied texts, when its larger effect was on the circulation of procedures. The distractors each claim an invention, equate a print run with an adoption, or read a place of origin off an archive's shelf.
questions.hint: Ask what a method needs before it can be used by somebody who has never seen it used.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A ledger that makes a claim checkable
questions.learningObjective: identify what a record kept for a court differs from one kept for a partner
questions.stem: A merchant who dies owing sums to several creditors leaves a disordered chest of papers, some of them his own memoranda, some correspondence, some scraps of a ledger. A relative compiles a summary of the debts for the court from these, and it is not accepted because it does not balance. Which account best explains the rejection?

options.text: The summary was not built from a self-checking record, so there is no way to find the error, and a court cannot accept a total it cannot reconcile
The summary was compiled by a relative, so the court required the compiler to be a sworn accountant
options.misconception: supplies a rule of court the rejection does not rest on

options.text: The merchant's own papers were informal, so the court required accounts drawn up in a standard printed form
options.misconception: invents a formal requirement the court did not impose

options.text: The chest was disordered, so the court rejected the summary because the original documents could not be produced in order
options.misconception: attributes the rejection to arrangement rather than to reconcilability

questions.explanation: The reason a court asks for balanced accounts is that balance is a test, and a summary assembled from loose papers is a collection of assertions that offers no way to locate the error, so the total cannot be checked by anyone including the person who computed it. A self-checking book answers a different question from a pile of memoranda, because it will not produce a total at all until every entry has found its other side, which means the total it produces has already survived a test. The compiler's relationship to the debtor and the disorder of the chest are both relevant to the difficulty of the task, but neither is what the rejection turns on, and a court that cared about either could require the compiler to attend and swear to the document. The distractors each substitute an administrative condition for the evidential one.
questions.hint: Ask what makes a total checkable by a person who did not compute it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A state that stopped paying and kept borrowing
questions.learningObjective: trace a repeated suspension of payments back to a settlement
questions.stem: A crown suspends payment on its short-term loans, the lenders stop advancing new sums, and after a year or two the crown offers a settlement in which a share of the arrears is converted into longer-term funded debt and the rest is paid in coin, and the lenders agree to lend again. Which feature of that sequence does the most to explain what a settlement is for?

options.text: It puts a stop to a run on the lenders by making them whole again, so lending resumes on a scale the crown could not have obtained by waiting
It converts a short-term liability into a permanent one, so the crown's annual burden falls and its total debt rises
options.misconception: treats the change of tenor as a change of the debt's size

options.text: It settles the question of whether the loans were valid, which the lenders had disputed since the suspension began
options.misconception: supposes a validity dispute the sequence does not mention

options.text: It obliges the lenders to lend at a lower rate in future, since the settlement is the price of their own access to the market
options.misconception: invents a condition the sequence does not state

questions.explanation: A settlement is what ends a run rather than what resolves a moral question, and its subject is the lenders' position. A crown that has stopped paying is a crown nobody wants to lend to, and a crown that nobody lends to cannot borrow, so the first thing a settlement must do is make the lenders whole enough to stop asking for cash. Once that is done the flow can resume, and the reason the crown needed a settlement rather than patience is that the lenders' refusal is a collective decision that does not lapse on its own, unlike an individual creditor's decision to wait. That is why such settlements are usually negotiated in a hurry and why their terms tend to look generous to the lenders relative to what the crown could have paid by waiting, if it could have paid at all. The distractors each confuse the tenor of the debt with its size, invent a dispute about validity, and supply a forward condition the text does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask what a crown needs the lenders to stop doing before it can borrow at all.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A state that stopped paying and kept borrowing
questions.learningObjective: weigh two explanations of lending to a known defaulter
questions.stem: A study of lending to a crown that suspended payment four times finds that before the third suspension the great majority of the lending came from firms that had lent before, and that across the suspensions the returns to lenders, measured over the whole period, were positive. One reading calls the crown a serial defaulter whose credit destroyed the value of its paper. Another calls it a borrower whose repeated but settled failures were priced into the rate and made lending to it profitable. Which statement about the pair is soundest?

options.text: The two readings are about different quantities, one the fate of a particular holder of paper and the other the return across the whole lending relationship, and both can be true at once
The second reading refutes the first, since a positive average return means no lender lost
options.misconception: confuses an average with every individual outcome

options.text: The first reading is right, since repeat lending by the same firms shows that they were unable to withdraw
options.misconception: treats repeat business as an absence of choice

options.text: The dispute is settled by the fact that the crown did repay at all, since a settlement proves the obligation was honoured
options.misconception: treats a negotiated rescheduling as full performance

questions.explanation: The two accounts are measuring at different levels, and the difference explains why the evidence appears to support both. A lender who held paper through a particular suspension and was paid in rescheduled funded debt rather than in coin on the day has been made worse in the short run by exactly the event that makes the whole relationship profitable, because the crown that defaults and then settles is one that needs lenders again and will pay a rate that includes the risk. Neither statement cancels the other: a positive average return across several decades is fully compatible with individual holders of short-term paper taking losses at each suspension, and the study's finding that most lending was repeat business is evidence about how the market priced the risk rather than about anybody's inability to withdraw. The distractors each collapse the two levels or mistake a rescheduled settlement for performance on the original terms.
questions.hint: Ask at what level of holding period each of the two figures is measured.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A state that stopped paying and kept borrowing
questions.learningObjective: connect the cost of war finance to the structure of a crown's debt
questions.stem: A crown's ordinary revenue is largely collected months after the start of the year, while its army must be paid weekly and its fleet must be paid on the day it sails. Suppose the crown covers the gap with short-term loans that it expects to repay out of the coming year's revenue, and one year the revenue arrives later than expected. Which consequence follows from the arrangement?

options.text: The crown's ability to meet a payment in one week depends on a sum it will not collect for several months, so a delay in the collection becomes a default rather than a shortage
The crown must borrow long-term, since short-term loans are by definition unsuitable for a gap between collection and payment
options.misconception: supplies a rule the arrangement does not observe

options.text: The lenders will simply wait, since a delay in collecting revenue is not a failure to repay
options.misconception: assumes patience the suspension shows is absent

options.text: The revenue is unaffected, since revenue collection and debt service are separate parts of the crown's finances
options.misconception: denies a connection the timing creates

questions.explanation: The arrangement is a timing mismatch, and a timing mismatch becomes a default the moment a forecast fails, which is what distinguishes it from a structural shortfall. The crown has promised a payment on a date certain, and the only thing standing behind the promise is an expected receipt that is not a receipt, so when the receipt is late the crown has no money on a day on which it has already promised money. That is why short-term borrowing at this scale needs a lender who can be paid quickly and a mechanism by which the lenders can coordinate their refusal, and it is why the resulting suspensions take the form of a declared stop rather than a series of individual failures. The distinction between a delay and a structural deficit matters throughout this material: a crown that is solvent on a multi-year view can still be unable to pay on a particular Tuesday. The distractors each supply a rule that the arrangement breaks, or deny the connection the timing creates.
questions.hint: Ask what is in the crown's account on the day it makes the promise.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A state that stopped paying and kept borrowing
questions.learningObjective: explain why a suspension travels between lenders
questions.stem: A crown suspends payment on its loans, and a group of lending houses in one city agrees among themselves to advance nothing further until terms are settled; the houses are not the crown's creditors but its correspondents, and the crown's payments normally run through them. Which feature explains why the crown's access to funds closes so quickly?

options.text: The houses sit on the payment route as well as on the credit route, so a collective refusal removes the channel through which the crown's money would have moved
The houses are the crown's creditors in substance, so their refusal is simply a refusal to lend
options.misconception: reduces a two-sided position to a single debt relationship

options.text: The crown has no other route for its payments, so the houses' agreement is legally void for want of a counterparty
options.misconception: supplies a legal doctrine the arrangement does not involve

options.text: The houses' agreement reduces the rate the crown pays, so a higher rate is what closes the channel
options.misconception: inverts the direction of the effect on the cost of funds

questions.explanation: The mechanism is that the same institutions are on both sides of the ledger, and that is what makes their agreement so much more than a decision about lending. A house that declines to advance credit also declines to pass on the payments with which other lenders would be repaid, and a crown that must move money through that house to service anything at all finds that a collective refusal removes not only new borrowing but the machinery for servicing the old. This is why such refusals were typically framed as a collective act among houses and why their duration is measured in the time it takes to move funds, rather than in the terms of any single loan. The crown's position is consequently worse than a simple default would suggest, and the settlement has to restore the channel rather than merely repay a sum. The distractors each collapse the two positions, invent a legal doctrine, and reverse the effect on the cost of funds.
questions.hint: Ask what else the same institutions do besides lend.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Pricing a risk that arrives once
questions.learningObjective: state what an underwriter is measuring
questions.stem: Sailors and merchants gather in a room over a coffee house, and an insurance broker offers to take a share of the risk of a voyage, quoting a rate that depends on the ship, the cargo, the season, the route and the record of losses on that route. Which feature of the quotation is the most consequential?

options.text: It is published, so a holder of the policy can see what others paid for a comparable risk and cannot plead ignorance of the price
It is negotiated, so each holder can bargain for a rate suited to the terms of the voyage
options.misconception: assumes rates are individually negotiated rather than quoted

options.text: It is fixed for the voyage, so a loss later in the season cannot change what the holder pays
options.misconception: supposes a premium can be revised after it is agreed

options.text: It is paid in advance, so an underwriter holds no risk between the agreement and the loss
options.misconception: denies the underwriter's exposure before a claim

questions.explanation: The publication of the rate is what turns the arrangement from a private bargain into a market, and it does more work than it first appears. An underwriter's problem is that the events are rare and the risks are dissimilar, so a price that is not visible cannot be tested: if every holder is told a different figure, no one can tell whether a high rate reflects a dangerous voyage or an inexperienced underwriter, and both parties are dependent on an assessment they cannot check. Publishing the figure solves that by supplying a common reference, and it is why these rates became the most valuable single record of the commercial world of the period, since they are contemporaneous, comparable and produced by parties with a financial interest in being believed. The arrangement's other features are real but secondary, and the premium is of course paid in advance precisely because the underwriter is exposed from that moment. The distractors each substitute a different market design or deny an exposure the arrangement creates.
questions.hint: Ask what a holder can do with a rate that nobody else has seen.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Pricing a risk that arrives once
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between mutualising a risk and pooling it
questions.stem: Suppose the people taking insurance on a voyage are the people whose own ships make that voyage, so that a loss falls on the others rather than on a stranger, and suppose the premiums paid are held and returned in good years. Which feature does that arrangement have, and what does it require?

options.text: The risk is mutualised among the participants, and it requires a reliable estimate of the aggregate frequency of loss so the contributions can be set
The risk is transferred to a stranger, and it requires that stranger to be better able to bear the loss than the participants
options.misconception: confuses mutualisation with transfer to a specialist

options.text: The risk is diversified by a fixed charge on every voyage, and it requires the state to guarantee the payments in a bad year
options.misconception: supplies a state guarantee the arrangement does not involve

options.text: The risk is eliminated by holding the premiums, and it requires the contributions to exceed the expected loss in every year
options.misconception: believes holding a fund removes the possibility of a loss

questions.explanation: Mutualising and pooling are different operations, and the distinction is worth holding because the early form of marine insurance is genuinely mutual while most of what followed is not. Where the participants cover one another, the arrangement is a rotation of risk, and what it needs is a shared estimate of how often losses occur, since the contributions have to be set against an expected frequency and there is no capital buffer to absorb a mistake. Where a stranger takes the risk for a premium, the arrangement is a transfer, and what it needs is capital, and the price at which the transfer is offered. The two can be combined, and often were, and a reader of a policy should be careful about which is in front of them, because the obligations of a mutual society and of a joint-stock insurer are not interchangeable. The distractors each substitute a different mechanism or add a party the arrangement does not name.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the loss, and what has to be estimated to set the contribution.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Pricing a risk that arrives once
questions.learningObjective: assess what a table of insurance rates can be used for
questions.stem: A surviving table of premiums sets out, for one year, the rate charged for voyages between named pairs of ports for hulls of stated tonnage, together with a separate schedule of what is not insured and an account of losses paid in the year. Read that table: which of the following uses does it support, and which does it not?

options.text: It supports a dated statement of what a specific voyage cost to insure, and it does not by itself support a statement of what the underlying risk objectively was
It supports a statement of the objective probability of loss, since the rate was set by underwriters who had the best information
options.misconception: treats a quoted price as a measurement of the underlying risk

options.text: It supports a statement of what goods were in the holds, since the schedule of exceptions names the cargoes involved
options.misconception: reads a statement about cover as a manifest of cargo

options.text: It supports a statement of how many voyages were made, since every voyage listed generated a policy
options.misconception: treats a list of quoted rates as a register of voyages

questions.explanation: A published rate is a price, and a price is a fact about a market rather than about the world. It supports the strongest possible claim about what a particular voyage cost to insure on a particular day, and about how the price varied with port, tonnage and season, which is exactly why these tables are among the best evidence in the period for the structure of a trade. What it does not support is a claim about the objective chance of loss, because the price reflects the underwriters' state of information, their capital, their appetite and what their competitors were charging, and those are all historical facts about a particular market. The exceptions and losses sections are about the contract and its outcome and not about the cargo, and a table of listed rates is not a register of voyages, since a voyage may have been insured by several writers or none. The distractors each promote the price into a probability, a manifest, and a register.
questions.hint: Ask whether a price is a measurement of the thing insured or of the market for insuring it.

questions.learningObjective: explain what a published rate does for the market that uses it
questions.stem: A market for insuring voyages develops in which the rates are printed in a list, the underwriters meet in one room, and a share of a risk can be taken by several of them for a share of the premium, so that no one underwriter's capital is committed beyond what it intends. A central bank that faces a speculative run on credit has to raise the price of money to defend its convertibility, and every business that borrows pays that higher price for as long as the defence lasts, so a boom in one asset class taxes the whole economy for as long as it continues. Legislators then legislate, restricting the formation of joint-stock companies or requiring a subscription that a later generation has to live with, and a formal restriction of that kind is very hard to remove because the firms licensed under it become established. A fourth transfer runs to the language: an episode acquires a name, and the name is then applied to episodes that share none of its features, which lowers the cost of naming and raises the cost of thinking. What does not transfer is any lasting improvement in the economy from the boom itself, since the capital raised during one went into uses fixed by the price structure that caused it, and several of those uses are still standing long after every share has been sold. The point for a reader is that the visible gain of a boom and the durable cost are borne by different people, which is the same asymmetry that shows up in a fiscal crisis, and it is why the story of a boom is mostly a story about what it did to everybody else.
